**Chapter 1**  
**THE PROBLEM AND ITS BACKGROUND**  
The growing demand for accessible and personalized fitness solutions has underscored the limitations of traditional fitness management practices, particularly in local community settings. This chapter presents the background of the study and establishes the research objectives, theoretical and conceptual frameworks, scope and limitations, significance of the study, and key terms that guide the development of SyncroFit: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set Recommendations.

**Project Context**  
The effective delivery of fitness guidance and management is essential in helping individuals maintain a healthy and consistent lifestyle, particularly within community-based gym environments. In LF Fitness Gym, current fitness management practices are still highly dependent on manual processes, verbal coaching, and generalized workout routines. Common issues experienced by clients include difficulty in identifying suitable exercises, lack of personalized workout planning, and inconsistent progress monitoring. Additionally, clients face limited knowledge regarding proper exercise execution, motivational struggles, and the absence of a structured digital platform for organizing workout activities and monitoring personal fitness progress.

For instance, beginners often rely on trial-and-error methods or seek repeated assistance from trainers to determine appropriate workouts, while progress tracking is commonly performed through memory, handwritten notes, or social media comparisons rather than through a structured monitoring system. Clients may also need to visit the gym or consult trainers directly to receive updates regarding workout routines, guidance, and fitness assessments, which can reduce flexibility and consistency in managing their fitness journey. These concerns highlight the need for an accessible mobile-based system that can provide structured exercise guidance, personalized workout recommendations, and convenient progress monitoring.

***![][image1]Figure 1-1. Fishbone Diagram of SyncroFit***

**Research Objectives**  
***General aim***   
The general aim of this study is to design, develop, and evaluate “SYNCROFIT: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set Recommendations” that provides users with personalized exercise sets based on their fitness goals, Body Mass Index (BMI), and fitness level.

***Specific Objectives***

1. To assess the current process of starting and managing a fitness journey in terms of workout planning, exercise selection, progress tracking, and challenges encountered by individuals.   
2. To design and develop a mobile-based fitness management application that provides users with personalized exercise sets based on their individual fitness goals, BMI, and fitness level.  
3. To compare the current manual fitness management process with the proposed automated system in terms of efficiency and user effectiveness.  
4. To assess the feasibility of implementing the proposed mobile-based fitness management application through cost-benefit analysis by evaluating its expected costs and benefits.  
5. To evaluate the technical quality of the application using the ISO/IEC 25010:2023 product quality model in terms of:  
   5.1. Functional Suitability;  
   5.2. Performance Efficiency;  
   5.3. Interaction Capability;  
   5.4. Reliability;   
   5.5. Security;

**Research Framework**  
***Theoretical Framework***  
	The study is primarily anchored on the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) developed by Fred D. Davis in 1989 \[56\], which explains user acceptance of information systems through the constructs of Perceived Usefulness (PU) and Perceived Ease of Use (PEOU). These beliefs influence users' attitudes and behavioral intentions toward using a system, which can ultimately contribute to actual system use.	  **![][image2]**

***Figure 1-2. Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) diagram***

**The Technology Acceptance Model (TAM)** as applied to SyncroFit illustrates how specific system features, such as personalized exercise sets, the BMI calculator, progress monitoring, and the simplified user interface, correspond to TAM constructs that influence user acceptance and continued system use.  
In this study, Perceived Usefulness is applied through SyncroFit's core features, particularly the generation of personalized exercise sets based on BMI, fitness goals, and fitness level, together with visual progress monitoring through timestamped photos that help users track physical changes over time. Perceived Ease of Use is demonstrated through SyncroFit's simplified user interface and streamlined profile setup flow, which are intended to maintain a user-friendly environment within the system.

The simplified presentation of user inputs and workout recommendations is intended to reduce information overload and help users understand how their fitness information is translated into personalized exercise sets. By providing an accessible interface and clearly presented workout plans, SyncroFit aims to promote a positive user experience and encourage users to incorporate the application into their regular fitness activities and workout tracking.

Existing studies on fitness application adoption and continued use emphasize the importance of perceived usefulness, ease of use, usability, and positive user experience in influencing users' willingness to adopt and continue using fitness applications \[1\], \[9\], \[12\]. These findings support the use of the Technology Acceptance Model (TAM) as an appropriate theoretical foundation for SyncroFit. Through personalized exercise recommendations, progress monitoring, and an accessible user interface, the application aims to enhance users' perception of usefulness and ease of use, which may contribute to user acceptance, continued engagement, and effective fitness management.  
***Conceptual Framework***  
The development of the proposed system, SyncroFit: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set Recommendations, follows an Input–Process–Output (IPO) framework that organizes the data gathered from users and research activities, the processes performed by the system, and the resulting features and outputs delivered to users.

***Figure 1-3. Input–Process–Output (IPO) Framework***

**Input Phase.** The input phase involves gathering data through client interviews at LF Fitness Gym, survey questionnaires administered to target respondents, and a review of related literature on fitness management and mobile health applications. User-specific inputs include personal information such as age, sex, height, and weight, together with the user's fitness goal and fitness level. Height and weight are used to determine the user's BMI, which serves as one of the parameters for generating personalized exercise recommendations.

**Process Phase.** The process phase focuses on the system's core computational and functional operations. This includes BMI calculation based on user-provided height and weight, the generation of personalized exercise sets using predefined rules aligned with the user's BMI category, fitness goal, and fitness level, and the implementation of progress tracking modules for workout logging, weight monitoring, and timestamped progress photos.

**Output Phase.** The output phase is a functional mobile-based fitness management application that provides personalized exercise set recommendations, visual progress reports, and structured workout schedules. The system enables users to organize their fitness routines, record and review their workout progress, and access personalized fitness guidance through an accessible mobile interface.

**Significance of the Study**  
This study presents a mobile-based approach to fitness management and personalized exercise tracking, focusing on workout organization, progress monitoring, and user engagement. The findings and developed application may benefit the following groups:  
**To LF Fitness Gym.** The application will serve as a supplementary tool that can support the gym in providing structured fitness guidance to its clients. By allowing users to access personalized exercise sets, manage workout routines, and monitor their own progress, SyncroFit can reduce repeated reliance on verbal guidance for basic workout planning while giving clients a more organized approach to managing their fitness activities.  
**To Gym Trainers.** The system can support trainers by providing users with automatically generated basic workout recommendations, which may reduce repetitive requests for general exercise guidance. This allows trainers to focus their attention on clients who require more specialized instruction, supervision, or professional assistance.  
**To Individuals for Home Workouts.** The application can serve as a fitness support tool for individuals who prefer exercising at home. SyncroFit provides personalized exercise sets, workout organization, and progress tracking features that can help users follow more structured fitness routines without depending solely on in-person guidance. These features may support home-based users in maintaining consistency, monitoring their progress, and working toward their fitness goals conveniently.  
**To Fitness Enthusiasts.** SyncroFit can support fitness enthusiasts by providing personalized exercise sets, workout tracking, and progress monitoring features in a single mobile application. These features may help users organize their fitness activities, review their progress, and maintain greater consistency in managing their workout routines.  
**To the Academic Community.** This study contributes to the body of knowledge in information technology and software engineering by demonstrating the practical application of mobile development, rule-based recommendation systems, and user-centered design principles in addressing real-world fitness management challenges.  
**To Future Researchers.** This study will serve as a useful reference for future innovations in fitness and health management systems. It demonstrates how mobile technology and rule-based recommendation systems can be applied to address challenges in personalized fitness management, workout guidance, and progress tracking, supporting further development of accessible digital fitness solutions.

**Scope and Limitation**  
The application is designed to allow users to track their workouts, monitor progress, and manage fitness activities conveniently through a mobile interface. SYNCROFIT also incorporates features such as progress visualization to help users monitor their development and support continued engagement with their fitness activities. The study will be limited to mobile platforms, specifically Android devices, and will involve testing with a selected group of gym members, fitness enthusiasts, and individuals who exercise at home. The evaluation will focus on the system's efficiency and user effectiveness, feasibility through cost-benefit analysis, and technical quality based on the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics.  
The system is intended for use by different categories of users, including individuals performing home workouts, fitness enthusiasts, gym members, and beginner users with limited exercise knowledge. These users will have access to core functionalities such as workout tracking, viewing personalized exercise sets, and progress monitoring. Exercise recommendations will be generated using user-provided information, with height and weight used to calculate BMI, together with the user's fitness goal and fitness level as the primary parameters for generating personalized exercise sets.  
However, the study is subject to certain limitations. SYNCROFIT will not include desktop, web-based, or iOS versions, as the application is specifically developed for Android devices. Its personalized exercise sets will depend on user-provided information and predefined rule-based logic using BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level rather than continuous physiological monitoring or professional medical assessment. The application will not provide real-time trainer interaction or live coaching features, and external integrations with wearable devices or third-party fitness applications will not be included in the initial version. Furthermore, the evaluation will be limited to a specific sample population, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to all fitness users. The system will not utilize artificial intelligence, machine learning, or deep learning algorithms to analyze user behavior patterns or predict fitness outcomes. Lastly, the study will focus on the application's efficiency, user effectiveness, feasibility, and technical quality based on the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 characteristics rather than long-term health outcomes or medical validation of the exercise routines.

**Definition of Terms**  
This section aims to provide a brief overview of key terms commonly used in the study. For better clarification and understanding of the terms, the following are defined conceptually and operationally. 

**Fitness Level. Refers to the user's self-identified level of fitness experience used by SyncroFit, together with BMI and fitness goal, as one of the parameters for generating personalized exercise sets.**  
**Fitness Goal.** Refers to the user's selected fitness objective in SyncroFit, which is used together with BMI and fitness level as one of the parameters for generating personalized exercise sets.  
**Body Mass Index (BMI).** A numerical value calculated using a person's height and weight that is used to classify weight status. In SyncroFit, the calculated BMI category serves as one of the parameters used in generating personalized exercise sets.  
**Fitness Application.** A software application designed to support users in planning, monitoring, and managing exercise-related activities and personal fitness progress.  
**Fitness Management.** The process of planning and monitoring exercise activities to achieve personal health and fitness goals.  
**Fitness Tracking.** Refers to the monitoring and recording of a user's fitness activities and progress through workout sessions, workout history, duration, weight records, and other progress-related information available within SyncroFit.  
**Progress Monitoring.** Refers to the process of recording and reviewing changes in a user's fitness-related data, workout activities, and performance over time.  
**Interaction Capability.** Refers to the ability of SyncroFit to support clear, understandable, and convenient interaction between the user and the application when accessing features, navigating the interface, and performing fitness-related tasks.  
**Mobile-Based Application.** Refers to the SyncroFit system developed specifically for Android devices, enabling users to access personalized exercise sets, workout tracking, progress monitoring, and other fitness management features through a mobile interface.  
**Personalized Exercise Set.** Refers to the customized workout routines generated by SyncroFit based on the user's BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level. The generated exercise set may also be modified by the user according to their exercise preferences.  
**Recommendation System.** Refers to the rule-based feature of SyncroFit that uses predefined conditions and user fitness information to generate personalized exercise recommendations without the use of artificial intelligence or machine learning.

**Chapter 2**  
**LITERATURE REVIEW**  
This chapter presents a review of related studies and literature that will support the development of SYNCROFIT: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set. It allows the researchers to obtain essential information by examining previous works, systems, and findings relevant to fitness management, mobile health applications, and personalized exercise technologies.

**Mobile Based Fitness Applications**  
Research studies indicate that the continued use of mobile fitness applications is mainly influenced by users' motivation, perceived usefulness, and ease of use. Studies have shown that users are more likely to continue using fitness applications when they find them helpful in achieving their fitness goals and when the applications are simple and convenient to use \[2\], \[12\]. In addition, several studies emphasize that a well-designed user interface and positive user experience are important factors in helping users stay engaged and achieve meaningful health outcomes \[9\], \[13\]. Furthermore, system quality and information quality within mobile fitness apps have been found to significantly affect user behavior and performance outcomes, reinforcing the importance of delivering accurate and well-structured content \[53\].  
Studies employed systematic reviews to provide a broad understanding of the factors influencing fitness app adoption and continued use \[1\], \[12\], \[25\]. Yang et al. \[25\] conducted a scoping literature review identifying key factors such as self-regulation, social influence, and perceived value as determinants of user adherence to physical activity applications. Other studies focused on the development and evaluation of specific fitness applications to assess their functionality and usability \[3\], \[9\]. A local study assessed the quality and use cases of mobile health applications in the Philippines during the COVID-19 pandemic, highlighting the growing importance of mobile health technologies in the local context \[23\]. Another study expanded the scope of mobile health applications by examining their effects on dietary behavior, showing that health-related mobile applications can support various aspects of personal wellness beyond exercise alone \[31\].  
The role of incentive mechanisms in sustaining user engagement has also been explored. Faizah et al. \[22\] investigated how incentive-based mobile fitness apps influence users' continuance intention, finding that rewards and recognition features can significantly enhance long-term app usage, with gender moderating these effects. Additionally, Xue et al. \[42\] examined how fitness app need support impacts women's exercise adherence behavior, revealing that self-efficacy and perceived health control serve as serial mediators in promoting sustained physical activity. Cross-sectional surveys have also provided empirical evidence on actual use patterns of smartphone apps supporting physical activity, demonstrating that users who actively engage with tracking features exhibit higher levels of physical activity compared to passive users \[63\]. Petersen et al. \[38\] conducted a randomised feasibility trial of two mobile health interventions for sedentary individuals, finding that app-based exercise programs are both feasible and acceptable for beginners who lack prior exercise habits.  
Overall, mobile fitness applications are more effective when they offer useful features, are easy to use, and provide a positive user experience. These findings are relevant to the present study because SyncroFit is designed to provide personalized exercise sets, workout tracking, and progress monitoring features that align with the characteristics commonly associated with successful mobile fitness applications.

**Exercise Adherence and Physical Activity Behavior**  
The suitability of the exercise program, and the ability to monitor progress over time plays a factor when it comes to user's motivation in exercise adherence. Studies indicate that individuals are more likely to continue exercising when they are provided with structured and personalized workout plans that align with their fitness goals and physical capabilities \[5\], \[11\], \[20\]. Sun et al. \[21\] further demonstrated that personalized mobile health apps employing enhanced action design research approaches can effectively motivate adherence to exercise plans by aligning app features with individual behavioral patterns.  
The reviewed studies differ in the technologies and approaches used to promote exercise adherence. Some studies focus on mobile applications that provide personalized exercise plans and progress monitoring to encourage users to remain active \[5\], \[11\], \[20\]. Dawson et al. \[24\] conducted a three-arm randomized controlled pilot trial examining the feasibility and acceptability of a mobile health exercise intervention for inactive adults, finding that mobile-delivered exercise programs are both feasible and well-received by previously sedentary individuals. Similarly, Zhang et al. \[44\] demonstrated through a randomized controlled trial that mHealth-based exercise interventions significantly improved the physical fitness of male college students with overweight and obesity, providing strong evidence for the effectiveness of mobile fitness interventions among young adult populations.  
Recent evidence further supports the effectiveness of app-based interventions in producing measurable fitness outcomes. Gomez-Cuesta et al. \[65\] conducted a randomized controlled trial showing that a mobile app-based intervention improved anthropometry, body composition, and fitness regardless of participants' previous active or inactive status. Wang and Zhao \[37\] also confirmed that smartphone-based fitness apps positively influence physical activity levels among users, reinforcing the role of mobile technology in promoting exercise behavior.  
In general, the findings suggest that users are more likely to adhere to exercise routines when they receive workout recommendations that are tailored to their goals and fitness level and when they can easily monitor their progress.

**Fitness Tracking and Monitoring Systems**  
Fitness tracking and monitoring systems are designed to help users record and evaluate their physical activity, workout intensity, and overall progress. Studies indicate that these systems are effective when they provide accurate data and present information in a way that is easy for users to understand \[4\], \[14\]. Mobile applications can serve as centralized platforms for storing and displaying progress information. Elder et al. \[14\] demonstrated that mobile applications can estimate exercise intensity even without external devices, showing that effective monitoring can be achieved using a smartphone alone.  
The use of mobile apps and fitness trackers to promote healthy behaviors has been examined through cross-sectional surveys, revealing that consistent use of tracking features is associated with higher physical activity levels and improved health outcomes \[32\]. Wang et al. \[46\] explored digital health interventions from the humanistic perspective of sports, emphasizing that tracking systems should not only collect data but also provide meaningful feedback that resonates with users' personal health goals and values.  
However, Richardson and Schulz \[61\] identified a critical challenge in fitness tracking systems: the "data-rich but guidance-poor" dilemma. Their analysis revealed that passive health and fitness tracking software often leads to user churn because while these systems collect extensive data, they fail to translate that data into actionable guidance. This finding directly supports the design rationale of SyncroFit, which combines tracking capabilities with personalized exercise recommendations to bridge the gap between data collection and meaningful fitness guidance.  
The studies make it clear that mobile apps can benefit when it comes to tracking workout progress, exercise frequency, and shifts in fitness level, even without wearable technology. The findings state that features like workout logs, BMI tracking, and timestamped progress pictures help users track their consistency and identify how frequently they engage in physical activity. This creates a sense of accountability and encourages users to maintain their routines.

**Personalized Exercise Recommendation Systems**  
The shift toward personalized fitness is driven by the need to match exercise routines with specific user profiles and preferences. Research indicates that tailored recommendations significantly enhance user engagement compared to generic plans \[6\].  
These systems often utilize user-centric data, such as body composition metrics and individual goals, to prescribe specific workouts \[8\], \[15\]. A key component of modern recommendation frameworks is the ability to adapt to the user's progress dynamically, ensuring that the physical activity remains relevant to their evolving fitness level \[7\], \[10\]. Furthermore, personalization has been identified as a critical factor in national health strategies to optimize physical outcomes across diverse populations \[18\]. Mehrabadi et al. \[29\] provided a comprehensive review of exercise recommendation systems, mapping the landscape of approaches from collaborative filtering to content-based methods, and identifying future directions for the field including the need for more accessible, user-friendly recommendation interfaces.  
Recent scoping reviews also highlight how these recommendation systems are increasingly integrated into mobile health (mHealth) interventions to support weight management and long-term behavioral changes \[16\], \[28\]. Notably, Bin Mohd Hairi \[58\] developed E-Fitness Buddy, a rule-based fitness mobile application that generates customized workout routines based on body metrics such as BMI, height, and weight. This system shares a similar approach with SyncroFit in utilizing rule-based logic and body composition parameters to deliver personalized exercise sets without requiring complex machine learning algorithms.  
Furthermore, Naliyatthaliyazchayil et al. \[49\] explored user perceptions of FitWisdom, an explainable and fairness-aware exercise recommender designed for clinical guideline adherence, demonstrating that transparency in how recommendations are generated significantly improves user trust and adoption. Johnston et al. \[59\] conducted a systematic review evaluating the clinical usability of exercise prescription apps, finding that apps with clear exercise instructions, appropriate difficulty progression, and user-friendly interfaces achieved the highest usability scores.

**Impact of Technology in Fitness Management**  
Technology has redefined how individuals manage their health by providing tools for real-time tracking and adherence monitoring. Mobile applications allow for precise exercise intensity tracking, which provides users with immediate feedback on their performance \[14\]. In the Philippines, the adoption of wearable technology and smartwatches has been influenced by user experience and perceived utility, showing a growing trend toward tech-integrated health management \[4\], \[23\].  
Beyond tracking, technology facilitates better adherence to fitness programs; for instance, football players using exercise apps showed improved aerobic endurance and consistency \[5\]. Park et al. \[47\] conducted a systematic review and meta-analysis of randomized controlled trials examining the effect of digital health applications with or without gamification on physical activity and cardiometabolic risk factors, finding that digital health interventions significantly increased physical activity levels regardless of gamification features.  
The integration of mobile apps with wearable devices creates a comprehensive ecosystem for health behavior change, allowing users to monitor a variety of health metrics in one place \[26\]. However, the success of these technological tools often depends on their alignment with quality standards, such as ISO 25010, which ensures software product quality and usability \[17\]. In this regard, S. B. et al. \[43\] applied the ISO/IEC 25010 framework to evaluate three mobile applications for reproductive health services, demonstrating the practical applicability of this quality model in assessing mobile health applications and providing a methodological precedent for SyncroFit's planned evaluation approach.

**Comparison of Traditional Fitness Methods and Digital Fitness Systems**  
Digital fitness systems offer a distinct alternative to traditional gym-based methods by providing flexibility and accessibility. Comparative studies suggest that fitness apps can serve as a valid alternative to traditional gyms, particularly for those seeking convenience \[30\]. More recent evidence confirms that digital interventions to promote physical activity among inactive adults improve health and well-being by being available, personalized, and adequate \[Sjoklint et al., 2023\]. While traditional face-to-face social interactions remain powerful motivators for physical activity, digital systems bridge the gap for insufficiently active college students by increasing self-efficacy and motivation through mobile interfaces \[34\].  
Digital systems also address common barriers found in traditional methods, such as the lack of personalized guidance and high costs, by offering automated exercise prescriptions \[35\]. Research among university students indicates that while gender can influence exercise intensity, the use of mobile apps generally leads to higher adherence compared to those relying solely on traditional, non-digital routines \[36\]. Rivera et al. \[60\] further evaluated the effectiveness of an mHealth application designed to promote home-based exercise in adults, providing evidence that mobile-delivered fitness programs can achieve comparable outcomes to supervised gym-based training while offering greater flexibility and accessibility.  
Additionally, Stevinson et al. \[19\] examined adherence and health-related outcomes of beginner running programs through a 10-week observational study, finding that structured programs with clear progression guidelines significantly improved adherence rates among beginners. While specific to running, these findings on beginner adherence patterns are transferable to general fitness contexts and support SyncroFit's approach of providing structured, progressive exercise sets for users new to fitness.  
Ultimately, digital systems enhance the "sense of presence" and continuous use intention, which are often harder to maintain in self-guided traditional fitness routines without a personal trainer \[27\], \[33\].

**Synthesis**  
The research gap identified by contrasting current fitness literature with the empirical findings from the client transcript reveals a deep separation between advanced health informatics and the operational realities of local community gyms. While academic literature assumes an ecosystem of cloud-synchronized databases, continuous automated tracking, and advanced machine learning algorithms, the target facility relies entirely on manual, physical logbooks for managing all membership and workout data ("lista-lista pa lang"). This absolute dependency on paper records creates a distinct literature gap regarding how standalone mobile solutions can practically mitigate manual data vulnerabilities, which currently manifest in severe record-keeping errors such as clients completely forgetting their exact enrollment timelines ("minsan nakakalimutan kailan sila nagstart"). Furthermore, the lack of digital data safety configurations leaves the facility completely unprotected against physical data loss, since information security is restricted to simply hiding the paper notebooks ("tinatago lang naman yan").  
A secondary critical research gap exists regarding the socio-economic accessibility of tailored workout programs within community fitness spaces. The reviewed literature emphasizes that personalized exercise sets dramatically optimize user self-efficacy, biological progression, and long-term adherence compared to generalized templates \[6\], \[21\], \[58\]. However, the client transcript highlights that real-world implementation introduces steep financial and structural barriers, as the local gym does not provide any digital or printed routine guides to clients ("sa ngayon wala pa eh") and actively gates personalized programming behind a separate premium fee ("another payment para sa special workout and guidelines"). Current software models fail to explore how automated, parameter-driven mobile systems can bypass these financial constraints to deliver free, immediate, and customized exercise recommendations directly to budget-conscious individuals or everyday gym beginners.  
Existing mobile health recommendations heavily assume stable, well-controlled training environments or dedicated one-on-one personal coaching, completely ignoring the structural and operational chaos of small-scale commercial gyms during high-traffic hours. According to the interview, when the facility reaches peak capacity, standard training management completely dissolves, forcing gym members to navigate the equipment entirely on their own ("pag puno na, kanya-kanya na lang ng diskarte"). Because the trainers are overwhelmed during these peak times, the gym's method of tracking physical development is reduced to an unrecorded, manual check on a weighing scale ("depende... sa timbang"). Richardson and Schulz \[61\] identified this exact phenomenon as the "data-rich but guidance-poor" dilemma in digital fitness contexts, yet no existing study addresses how a decentralized, user-led mobile tracking tool can maintain structured fitness tracking when human supervision is unavailable. There is an immediate shortage of empirical research focusing on a mobile application equipped with active session timers and chronological progress journals to maintain consistent, structured fitness tracking in unsupervised environments, directly fulfilling the exact data-driven tracking upgrades desired by local stakeholders.

**Chapter 3**  
**METHODOLOGY**  
This chapter presents the systematic approach employed in the analysis, design, development, and evaluation of SyncroFit: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set Recommendations. The study adopts an object-oriented approach to system development, utilizing the Agile methodology to ensure iterative and incremental delivery of system features.

**Research Design**  
In this study, the researchers adopted a descriptive quantitative research design to evaluate the proposed SyncroFit application. This approach enables the researchers to collect and analyze numerical data from respondents through survey questionnaires and system evaluation instruments. The evaluation focuses on the system's efficiency and user effectiveness, implementation feasibility, and technical quality based on the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 product quality characteristics.

**Research Locale**  
***![][image3]***  
***Figure 3-1. Map of Brgy. Canlubang, Calamba Laguna particularly Kapayapaan Ville***

The study was conducted at LF Fitness Gym located in Kapayapaan Ville, Barangay Canlubang, Calamba City, Laguna. The locale was selected because it provides access to gym clients and fitness-related practices relevant to the study, allowing the researchers to gather contextual information regarding workout planning, exercise guidance, and progress monitoring.

**Population and Participants of the Study**   
The study involves selected respondents representing the intended users of SyncroFit, including gym members, fitness enthusiasts, individuals who perform home workouts, and beginners with limited exercise knowledge. These participants are considered appropriate because they have experience or interest in workout planning, exercise selection, and progress monitoring and can provide relevant feedback regarding the proposed application.

**Sampling Technique**  
The study uses purposive sampling to select respondents who meet the characteristics relevant to the study. Participants are selected based on their involvement or interest in fitness-related activities and their ability to provide relevant information and feedback regarding workout management and the use of a mobile fitness application.

**Instruments of the Study**  
The study employs interviews, a review of related studies and literature, survey questionnaires, and system evaluation instruments to gather the information required for the development and evaluation of SyncroFit. These instruments are used to identify existing fitness-management challenges, determine user needs, and evaluate the developed application based on the objectives of the study.

**Interviews.** Interviews will be primarily conducted by the researchers in the study to gather deeper insights regarding the experiences, preferences, and challenges faced by individuals in maintaining their fitness routines. 

**Process Analysis.**

**Related Studies.** The researchers reviewed previous studies, published journals, fitness guidelines, and existing mobile fitness applications to guide the development of the proposed system. These sources helped identify common limitations in existing fitness applications, determine appropriate system features, and establish the basis for the rule-based generation of personalized exercise sets according to the user's fitness goal, Body Mass Index (BMI), and fitness level.

**Survey Questionnaires.** Survey questionnaires are used at different stages of the study. A needs-assessment questionnaire gathers quantitative information regarding respondents' fitness habits, exercise frequency, challenges in maintaining workout routines, and preferred mobile fitness features. A post-development system evaluation questionnaire is used to gather user feedback on SyncroFit's efficiency and user effectiveness and to evaluate the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 product quality characteristics.

**Data Analysis**  
The study uses descriptive analysis for interview data and descriptive quantitative methods for survey and system-evaluation data. The results are organized according to the research objectives to support the assessment of the current process, system development, comparative evaluation, feasibility, and technical quality of SyncroFit.

**Software Development Methodology**

**![][image4]**  
***Figure 3-2. Agile Model***

Figure 3-2 illustrates the Agile Model adopted for the development of SyncroFit. Agile allows the researchers to develop the application incrementally through iterative cycles called sprints, while continuously refining system features and interface designs based on testing outcomes and user feedback. This methodology promotes frequent evaluation and modification of functionalities to ensure that the proposed system remains aligned with the intended objectives and user needs. The Agile approach was selected because it accommodates changing requirements, supports rapid prototyping, and enables the development team to deliver functional increments at the end of each sprint cycle.

**System Overview**  
The proposed system is designed to help users manage their fitness routines by providing personalized exercise sets based on their fitness goals, Body Mass Index (BMI), and fitness level. In addition to generating personalized exercise sets, the application includes customizable exercise sets, workout scheduling and logging, progress monitoring through timestamped progress photos and weight logs, and a community forum for sharing progress and interacting with other users. By integrating these features into a single mobile platform, SyncroFit provides users with a structured and convenient approach to fitness management.  
The proposed system is intended for individuals who perform home workouts, fitness enthusiasts, gym members, and beginners with limited exercise knowledge. These users may encounter challenges in selecting appropriate exercises, organizing workout routines, and consistently tracking their progress. To address these concerns, SyncroFit offers a BMI calculator, rule-based personalized exercise recommendations, workout scheduling and logging, progress photo tracking, a community forum, and the ability to personalize recommended exercise sets according to user preferences.

**Phase 1\. Planning**  
To gather the necessary information for the development of the system, the researchers planned to conduct a review of related literature and studies and to administer a survey questionnaire to potential users. The survey focused on identifying the challenges encountered in managing fitness routines, the limitations of existing fitness applications, and the features respondents considered most useful in a mobile fitness application.

The system's functional requirements include user authentication, profile management, BMI calculation, rule-based personalized exercise recommendations based on BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level, exercise set customization, workout scheduling and logging, progress photo uploads, weight and progress monitoring, a progress dashboard, and a community forum module. The system's non-functional requirements are evaluated using the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 product quality characteristics: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Interaction Capability, Reliability, and Security.

The Planning phase served as the foundation for succeeding Agile iterations by ensuring that the proposed system was aligned with both the study objectives and the needs of potential users.

**Phase 1.2 Flowchart of Current Process**

**![][image5]**  
***Figure 3-3. Flowchart of Current Process of Starting or managing fitness journey.*** 

	**Figure 3-3** The current process of starting and managing a fitness journey at LF Fitness Gym begins when an individual decides to pursue fitness goals such as weight loss, muscle gain, or overall health improvement. Based on the client interview transcript, users proceed by inquiring about gym membership and receiving an initial consultation from trainers, which is often informal and based on basic assessment of their goals and fitness level. After this, a generalized workout routine is assigned, which the client follows during gym visits with minimal personalization. The transcript further highlights that clients often rely on trial-and-error adjustments, verbal feedback from trainers, and manual methods such as notes or memory to track their progress. Overall, the process is repetitive and largely manual, relying heavily on in-person guidance and lacks a structured or system-based fitness monitoring approach.   
**Phase 2\. System Design**  
***![][image6]***  
***Figure 3-4A. Proposed System Flowchart***

**Figure 3-4A** illustrates the system checks whether the user already has an account. If the user does not have an account, they are directed to the registration page where the user enters personal details such as age, sex, height, and weight. After submitting the required information, the profile is saved to the system. If the user has an account, they are directed to the sign-in page. Once the user is signed-in, they are directed to the dashboard of the system where the user can select the profile module to edit personal information, the progress module to check the progress of the user’s workouts and upload progress photos, and the plan module wherein the user is able to select their schedule of workout, receive recommended exercise sets, and modify the recommended exercise sets.

**![][image7]**  
***Figure 3-4B. Proposed System Flowchart***

**Figure 3-4B** illustrates the profile module, where users can view and update their personal information. The system retrieves the user's height and weight and calculates the Body Mass Index (BMI). The computed BMI and other profile information are displayed to the user. The user's fitness goal and fitness level, together with BMI, serve as the core profile parameters used in generating personalized exercise recommendations. The settings option is also available within this module, allowing users to configure application preferences and log out of the system.

 **![][image8]**  
***Figure 3-4C. Proposed System Flowchart***

**Figure 3-4C** demonstrates the progress module, which enables users to monitor their fitness development through three sections: Overview, Weight, and Photos. The Overview section displays the total number of completed workout sessions and their duration.  The Weight section allows users to input their current weight, which is stored with a timestamp for historical tracking. Lastly, the Photos module allows users to upload progress photos, which are also stored with timestamps for visual comparison over time. These features help users monitor both numerical and physical changes throughout their fitness journey. 

**![][image9]**  
***Figure 3-4D. Proposed System Flowchart***

**Figure 3-4D** illustrates the workout plan module. The system uses the user's BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level as the core parameters for personalized exercise generation. The user selects a preferred workout schedule and may specify available equipment as well as preferred or excluded exercises before initiating generation. When the user presses the Generate Workout button, the system produces a schedule-aware personalized exercise set based on the user's profile, schedule, available equipment, and exercise preferences.  
The user may either accept the generated workout plan or customize it according to their preferences. Once the workout plan is finalized, the user can view the workout schedule and begin the workout session. After completing the exercises, the session is marked as completed and stored in the system.

**![][image10]**  
***Figure 3-5. Data Flow Diagram Level 0***

**Figure 3-5** presents the Level 0 Data Flow Diagram of SyncroFit and illustrates the exchange of information between the user and the system. The user provides account and profile information, including height, weight, fitness goal, fitness level, workout availability or schedule, available equipment, exercise preferences, and workout-related data. Height and weight are used to calculate BMI. The system uses BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level as the core recommendation parameters, while the selected schedule, available equipment, and preferred or excluded exercises are used to refine the generated exercise set. Workout logs, weight records, and progress photos are processed to provide progress information and dashboard summaries.

It shows the relationships between the main entities such as User, Profile, Exercise, Personalized Exercise Set, and Workout Log. The diagram illustrates how user information, workout records, and personalized exercise recommendations are stored and connected within the database to support fitness tracking and management.

***Figure 3-27 . Gantt Chart***

**Figure 3-27** illustrates the Gantt Chart of SyncroFit: A Mobile-Based Fitness Management Application with Personalized Exercise Set Recommendations. It presents the major activities undertaken throughout the project, including problem and requirements analysis, data gathering, project planning, wireframe design, system development, testing, deployment, and feedback. The development phase involved the implementation and integration of the application's core features, followed by iterative testing and refinement to identify functional, interface, and integration issues. Android builds of the application are used for system evaluation, while feedback gathered during testing and evaluation supports further improvements to the system.

**Phase 3.1 Technology Stack**  
This section presents the technologies used in the development of SyncroFit, categorized into frontend, backend, and database layers based on their specific roles and functions in building and operating the system.

**Dart with Flutter Framework.** Dart serves as the primary programming language used in conjunction with the Flutter framework for developing the mobile application's frontend. Flutter is an open-source UI software development kit that enables the creation of a responsive and visually consistent user interface using a single codebase for Android devices. The framework provides a rich set of pre-built widgets and supports hot reload functionality, which accelerates the development process and allows for rapid iteration of UI components.

**PHP with Laravel Framework.** PHP serves as the backend programming language, utilized through the Laravel framework to build the application's RESTful API server. Laravel provides a structured and elegant approach to handling HTTP requests, database operations, authentication, and routing. The framework's built-in features such as Eloquent ORM, middleware, and migration tools streamline backend development and ensure maintainable, scalable server-side logic for managing user data, exercise records, and recommendation processing.

**MySQL.** MySQL serves as the primary server-side relational database management system of SyncroFit and stores persistent application data such as user profiles, exercise information, workout plans, workout records, progress data, community-related data, and parameters used by the rule-based recommendation system. During local development, the Laravel backend and MySQL database are managed through Laragon, which serves as the researchers' local development environment. Laragon is not used as the production hosting platform. For deployed and evaluation builds, the mobile application communicates with the hosted Laravel API, which handles server-side operations and access to the application's persistent database.

**SQLite (On-Device Cache).** SQLite is implemented as the on-device local database for offline caching and data synchronization. This lightweight database engine allows the application to store user profile data, workout schedules, and exercise sets locally on the device, enabling users to access their fitness plans and log workouts even without an active internet connection. When connectivity is restored, the locally cached data is synchronized with the MySQL server database to maintain data consistency across sessions.

**GitHub.** GitHub is used as the version control platform for managing the source code repository, tracking changes, and maintaining a history of all development iterations throughout the project lifecycle.

**Figma.** Figma is used as the primary UI/UX design tool for creating wireframes and high-fidelity mockups of the application's interface before translating them into Flutter code during the development phase.

**Phase 3.2 Agile Sprint Breakdown**

The development of SyncroFit follows an Agile methodology with iterative sprint cycles. Each sprint focuses on delivering specific functional increments of the system. The sprint breakdown is documented through the project's GitHub commit history, which serves as verifiable evidence of the development timeline and progress.

**Sprint 1: UI Development (July 14, 2026\)**  
The first sprint focused on converting the Figma wireframe designs into functional Flutter code. This included the implementation of the core user interface screens such as the sign-in page, sign-up page, home dashboard, navigation structure, and the overall visual layout of the application. The goal of this sprint was to establish the foundational UI framework upon which subsequent features would be built.

**Sprint 2: UI Improvements and Profile Navigation (July 22, 2026\)**  
The second sprint refined the user interface based on initial testing and added the user profile sidedrawer navigation component. This sprint improved the overall user experience by implementing smoother navigation flows, enhancing visual consistency across screens, and integrating the profile section with the application's global navigation structure.

**Sprint 3: Backend Development v1.0 — Authentication and Database Setup (July 26–28, 2026\)**  
The third sprint established the backend infrastructure of the system. This included setting up the Laravel API server, configuring the MySQL database via Laragon, implementing user registration and login authentication endpoints, and resolving database connection issues encountered during initial integration. Phase 2 of this sprint specifically addressed database connection fixes to ensure stable communication between the Flutter frontend and the Laravel backend API.

**Sprint 4: Offline Support and Profile Synchronization (August 4–10, 2026\)**  
The fourth sprint implemented the offline capability of the application using SQLite as the local cache database. This sprint enabled users to access their profile data and workout information without an active internet connection. Additionally, the profile saving mechanism was developed along with the offline synchronization feature, which ensures that locally stored data is properly synced with the MySQL server when connectivity is restored. Minor tweaks and bug fixes were also applied to stabilize the system.

**Sprint 5: Progress Tracking and Profile Improvements (September 6, 2026\)**  
The fifth sprint focused on implementing and refining the application's progress tracking and profile-management features. This included workout logging and history, weight progress tracking with timestamped entries, timestamped progress photo uploads with chronological organization, and improvements to the user's profile information and editing functions. Progress information was also integrated into the application dashboard to allow users to review their fitness activities over time.

**Sprint 6: Personalized Exercise Recommendations (September 7-9, 2026\)**  
The sixth sprint focused on the core personalized exercise recommendation feature of SyncroFit. The system calculates the user's Body Mass Index (BMI) from their recorded height and weight and uses BMI, fitness goal, and fitness level as the core parameters for the rule-based recommendation process. Workout availability or schedule, available equipment, and preferred or excluded exercises are also considered to refine the generated exercise set. Workout generation is initiated by the user through the Generate Workout action, after which the user can review, customize, regenerate, and accept the generated plan. The sprint also integrated the active workout flow, including exercise-set completion, workout timing, rest periods, and workout-session summaries.

**Sprint 7: Community Module and System Integration (September 11-15, 2026\)**  
The seventh sprint focused on the implementation and integration of the community module. The module provides users with a space to interact with other SyncroFit users through community-related features and fitness discussions. The sprint also included integration and refinement activities to ensure that the community module works consistently with user authentication, profiles, navigation, and the other major features of the application.

**Phase 4\. Testing**  
The testing phase involves iterative evaluation of SyncroFit to identify functional, interface, integration, and data-related issues throughout development. Functional testing is performed on implemented modules including user authentication, profile management, BMI calculation, personalized exercise-set generation, exercise-set customization, workout scheduling and logging, active workout sessions, progress monitoring, and community features. Integration testing verifies communication between the Flutter mobile application and the Laravel backend API, including the proper storage and retrieval of data from the MySQL database. Offline functionality and synchronization are also tested to verify that locally cached information can be accessed and synchronized appropriately when network connectivity becomes available.

Following functional and integration testing, the developed application is evaluated by selected respondents. Its technical quality is assessed using the selected ISO/IEC 25010:2023 product quality characteristics: Functional Suitability, Performance Efficiency, Interaction Capability, Reliability, and Security. User evaluation is also used to assess the system's efficiency and user effectiveness in comparison with the current manual fitness-management process.

**Phase 5\. Deployment**  
SyncroFit is deployed as an Android application for installation and system evaluation on compatible Android devices. Evaluation builds communicate with the hosted Laravel API, which manages server-side processing and access to the application's persistent database. Selected respondents are provided with the necessary installation and usage instructions to enable them to use and evaluate the application in an actual mobile environment. Deployment for research evaluation is distinguished from the application's final public production release, which may require additional release preparation such as final build configuration, signing, packaging, and distribution.

**Phase 6\. Feedback and Maintenance**  
Following deployment and system evaluation, feedback from respondents and testing results is reviewed to identify issues and areas for improvement. Maintenance activities include correcting identified bugs, refining application features and user-interface elements, updating exercise-related content when necessary, and maintaining compatibility with supported Android versions. Feedback gathered from the evaluation also serves as a basis for future refinements to SyncroFit while preserving the scope and limitations established for the study.

**Ethical Consideration**  
In conducting this study, the researchers observed the ethical principles of respect, beneficence, and justice to ensure that the rights and welfare of the respondents will be protected throughout the research process. The respondents will be informed about the purpose of the study, its objectives, and how their responses would be used in the development of the proposed system. 

Respondents will be given the option to decline participation or discontinue answering the interview and survey questionnaire at any time without any penalty or negative consequences. To protect their privacy, the survey did not require respondents to provide sensitive personal information beyond what was necessary for the study. This study will comply with the provisions of Republic Act No. 10173, also known as the Data Privacy Act of 2012, which mandates the responsible collection, processing, and protection of personal information.
